senses: Tenualosa ilisha, a fish in the herring family, and a popular food fish in South Asia.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi हिल्सा (hilsā).

senses: Anything that flattens.
ety: From flatten + -er.

senses: An exercise where the pupil is instructed to repeat a previously played rhythm by clapping.
A witty or sarcastic retort.
ety: Deverbal from clap back. Compare similarly formed Middle English ȝainclappe (“counterblow, riposte”, literally “back-clap”).
examples: While these bits of online affirmation are addicting, so too are the online takedowns, the clapbacks, the snark.

senses: The official currency of Sweden.
ety: Borrowed from Swedish krona (“crown”). Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, króna, and krone.

senses: Any of a set of visual symbols representing concepts or aphorisms, originally created by the Akan of Ghana and the Gyaman of Côte d'Ivoire in West Africa, often used as artistic devices.
ety: Borrowed from Akan adinkra.

senses: Actually existing.
ety: From subsist + -ent.

senses: A porter in Turkey and nearby countries.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic حَمَّال (ḥammāl, “porter”).

senses: Having coils; coiling.
ety: From coil + -y.
examples: The pillars in Figure 12.24 were built similarly: I designed a helix (a coily cord shape) and then swept a large 2D circle along the path the helix describes.

senses: Coloured or marked with red; placed in rubrics.
ety: From Middle English rubriche, rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rūbrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

senses: wildness, spirit, courage, ferocity
A cognatic descent group.
ety: Borrowed from French ramage, from Middle French and Old French ramage, from ram (“branch”) + -age. by surface analysis, rame + -age.

senses: Painful, hurtful; that is expressed by the word ouch.
ety: From ouch + -y.
examples: This is ouchy pain like breaking your leg, not heartache pain like when 'N Sync broke up and left me with nothing.

senses: A particular phenomenon of visual perception, the ganzfeld effect.
ety: From German, meaning "complete field", from ganz + Feld.

senses: An Italian or Provençal song or ballad.
A canzona (mediaeval Italian instrumental composition).
ety: From Italian canzone (“song”), from Latin cantiō. Doublet of cantion and chanson.

senses: To show elation or triumph; to rejoice.
ety: Either a back-formation from jubilation, or borrowed from Latin iūbilātus, perfect passive participle of iubilō (“to shout for joy”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

senses: Any of several muscles whose contraction causes the raising of a part of the body.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin levātor (“one that lifts or raises”). Doublet of lever.

senses: father, papa.
ety: Alteration of papa.

senses: The particles or radiation deflected in this manner.
ety: Back-formation from backscattering.

senses: A game in which an opponent is defeated by a sizable margin; a blowout.
A variety of the domestic pigeon.
ety: From Middle English lawȝar, lawher(e); equivalent to laugh + -er.

senses: The variety of configurations of the brain, especially with regard to autism.
ety: From neuro- (prefix denoting the nervous system) + diversity, coined by the Australian sociologist Judy Singer (born 1951) in her Bachelor of Arts dissertation (1998), and popularized by Harvey Blume in The Atlantic in September 1998: see the quotations.

senses: A soul patch, especially in a historical (pre-modern) context.
Small stickers or patches affixed to the face as a beauty mark.
ety: From French mouche. Doublet of Musca.
examples: They lent him a worn aspect which not even a fiercely erect little mustache and a tiny mouche beneath the lower lip could counteract.
The hair and beard are represented by a plastic mass : the mouche under the lower lip radiates outward and the moustache consists of two separate strands ending in spirals.
In the colonial period, the taste for red lips and cheeks came and went, as did fashions for mouches and wigs.

senses: Having to do with the area inside a lesion.
ety: From intra- + lesional.
examples: An injection which is administered directly into a cancerous area is an intralesional injection.

senses: The study of icons in art or art history.
ety: From Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “icon”) + -logy.

senses: A flat tapestry-woven carpet or rug from Turkey or Kurdistan.
ety: Borrowed from Turkish kilim, from Persian گلیم (gelim), akin to Aramaic גלימא (galīmā, “blanket, garment, cloth”), both from Ancient Greek κάλυμμα (kálumma, “cover, top, covering”) derived from καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”).

senses: The practice or tendency of catastrophizing, regarding bad things as catastrophic.
ety: From catastrophe + -ism, coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1837.
examples: A therapeutic programme based on pain education showed significant improvements regarding pain intensity, disability, catastrophism, depression, anxiety and health, with few positive results on anguish and cognition.

senses: A soft cow's-milk cheese from France and Switzerland.
A cake-shaped dessert made of an almond paste shell filled with (non-frozen) double cream and topped with whipped cream.
ety: Borrowed from French vacherin, from Franco-Provençal [Term?]. The dessert was likely named for its resemblance to the round shape of vacherin cheese wheels.
examples: After all, the lure of endless, sensual evil is as nothing compared to a good, spoonable Vacherin.

senses: An operatic song in slow tempo, either complete in itself or (e.g., in Bellini and Verdi) followed by a faster, more resolute section: hence
ety: From Italian cavatina, diminutive of cavata.

senses: A section of a long narrative poem; a canto
ety: Borrowed from Latin passus, the active participle of pandere.

senses: Something that lacks homogeneity.
A local departure from homogeneity.
ety: From in- + homogeneity.
examples: Other inhomogeneities in the ensemble of quantum dots are considered to make the optical spectrum of the levels broad.

senses: Of or resembling the moon; symbolized by the moon.
ety: From moon + -ed.

senses: The stems and leaves of the coriander plant, Coriandrum sativum, used as a seasoning and garnish in cooking.
ety: From Spanish cilantro, possibly from an unattested regional Vulgar Latin variant (with a front vowel) of Late Latin coliandrum, from Latin coriandrum (“coriander”). Doublet of coriander and culantro.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a vamp; tending toward indecency.
ety: From vamp + -y (adjectival suffix).
examples: She was a wonderfully campy, vampy siren, and her double fouettes in the coda were breathtaking.
Except that Evil Jeannie was a vampy, trampy slut, who goes around seducing another Air Force officer, named Biff, in the episode “My Sister, The Homewrecker.”

senses: Obtained by crowdsourcing.
ety: From crowd + sourced.
examples: The movement took on its modern form as it grew together with hackerspaces, crowdsourced science projects and online forums.

senses: To dress up or decorate in a showy way.
ety: First use appears c. 1952, apparently from Gussy (an adjective), schoolyard slang for “overly dressed” (1940); perhaps related to gussie (“an effeminate man”) (1901) and somehow connected to Gussie, the nickname for Augusta and Augustus.

senses: A member of an order of ascetic monks in parts of India
A monastery used by this order
ety: Borrowed from Hindi अखाड़ा (akhāṛā).

senses: A compression; the packing together of loose matter.
Something packed together tightly; a mass of densely-packed matter.
ety: From Latin impingere (“to dash against, impinge”).

senses: that jingles, having a jingling sound.
ety: From jingle + -y.

senses: A small bag, especially a small, clear, plastic bag.
ety: From bag + -ie (diminutive suffix).

senses: The act of genuflecting.
ety: Borrowed from Latin genuflexio, though with standardized spelling. By surface analysis, genuflect (“to bend the knee”) + -ion (Latinate abstract-noun suffix).
examples: Certain business titans have made Mar-A-Lago a scene of such flagrant self-abnegation, ring-kissing, and genuflection that it would embarrass a medieval Pope.

senses: A belief that spirits inhabit some or all classes of natural objects or phenomena.
A belief that an immaterial force animates the universe.
A doctrine that animal life is produced by an immaterial spirit.
ety: From anima + -ism, from Latin anima (“life", "breath", "soul”). Dated sense from German Animismus, coined c. 1720 by physicist/chemist Georg Ernst Stahl (1660-1734) See anima mundi.

senses: To establish a standard consisting of regulations for how something is to be done across an organization.
To make to conform to a standard.
To check for conformance with a standard.
ety: From standard + -ise.
